lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
description: 20 Consolidated Unique USMLE-Style Clinical Vignette Practice Problems (1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 5th Order) with No IDs

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 70-kg healthy male is admitted for an elective surgical procedure. The surgical resident calculates his baseline fluid compartments based on standard physiological estimates. Assuming total body water (TBW) constitutes approximately 60% of his total body weight, which of the following is the estimated volume of fluid normally contained within his intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment?
usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Total body water (TBW) comprises approximately 60% of total body weight (0.60 x 70 kg = 42 L). According to the standard 60-40-20 distribution rule, intracellular fluid (ICF) accounts for two-thirds (2/3) of total body water (or 40% of total body weight), which corresponds to 28.0 L (42 L x 2/3 = 28 L). The remaining one-third (1/3) of TBW resides in the extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment (14.0 L).

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 28-year-old female presents to the urgent care clinic with severe secretory watery diarrhea and vomiting for 24 hours. Physical examination reveals dry oral mucosa, sunken eyes, and poor skin turgor. Orthostatic vitals show a 26 mm Hg systolic drop upon standing. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates an elevated hematocrit of 52% (baseline: 40%) and an increased plasma protein concentration of 8.8 g/dL (reference: 6.0–8.0 g/dL). Serum sodium and calculated serum osmolality are within normal limits at 140 mEq/L and 290 mOsm/kg, respectively. Following complete osmotic equilibration, which of the following combinations of changes in extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, intracellular fluid (ICF) volume, and intracellular fluid osmolarity has occurred in this patient?

options.A: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume decreased, ICF osmolarity increased
options.B: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume unchanged, ICF osmolarity unchanged
options.C: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume increased, ICF osmolarity decreased
options.D: ECF volume increased, ICF volume unchanged, ICF osmolarity unchanged
options.E: ECF volume unchanged, ICF volume decreased, ICF osmolarity increased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Secretory diarrhea involves the loss of approximately isosmotic fluid from the extracellular compartment (isosmotic volume contraction). ECF volume decreases, but because the lost fluid is isosmotic to normal plasma, the osmolarity of the remaining ECF is unchanged. Because no transcellular osmotic gradient is created, there is no driving force for water movement between the ECF and ICF; thus, ICF volume and ICF osmolarity remain unchanged. The hematocrit and plasma protein concentration increase solely due to hemoconcentration within the contracted vascular/ECF space.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 34-year-old male endurance hiker becomes lost in the desert during summer and is rescued after 48 hours without access to drinking water. Physical examination reveals marked lethargy, dry mucous membranes, and tachycardia. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates hypernatremia (serum sodium: 158 mEq/L) and hyperosmolality (serum osmolality: 325 mOsm/kg; reference: 275–295 mOsm/kg). Serum total protein concentration is elevated at 9.4 g/dL. However, a complete blood count reveals a hematocrit of 45%, which is essentially unchanged from his pre-expedition baseline. Which of the following mechanisms best explains why this patient's hematocrit remained approximately unchanged despite severe volume contraction?

options.A: Concomitant splenic sequestration of erythrocytes balanced the plasma volume loss
options.B: Osmotic shrinkage of erythrocytes offset the hemoconcentrating effect of decreased plasma volume
options.C: Transient suppression of erythropoiesis blunted reticulocyte release
options.D: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure forced intact erythrocytes into the interstitium
options.E: Renal tubular retention of free water selectively expanded red blood cell volume

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: In hyperosmotic volume contraction (water deprivation/hypotonic sweat loss), the primary loss of free water elevates ECF osmolarity, which draws water out of the ICF down its osmotic gradient. While the loss of plasma volume normally concentrates erythrocytes and increases hematocrit, the hypertonic ECF concurrently causes water to leave erythrocytes, causing individual red blood cells to shrink (decreasing RBC volume). These two opposing forces—decreased plasma volume (which elevates hematocrit) and decreased erythrocyte volume (which lowers hematocrit)—offset each other, resulting in an essentially unchanged hematocrit despite hemoconcentration of plasma proteins.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 42-year-old female with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) presents to the emergency department with profound fatigue, postural hypotension, and generalized hyperpigmentation. Due to non-compliance with her fludrocortisone replacement therapy, she has experienced excessive renal sodium wasting. Laboratory evaluation shows severe hyponatremia (serum sodium: 118 mEq/L), hypovolemia, elevated hematocrit, and elevated plasma protein concentration. If a Darrow-Yannet diagram were constructed to depict her body fluid compartments following osmotic equilibration, which of the following shifts in the dimensions (width and height) of the intracellular fluid (ICF) and extracellular fluid (ECF) compartments would be observed relative to normal baseline?

options.A: ECF width decreased, ECF height decreased, ICF width increased, ICF height decreased
options.B: ECF width decreased, ECF height increased, ICF width decreased, ICF height increased
options.C: ECF width decreased, ECF height unchanged, ICF width unchanged, ICF height unchanged
options.D: ECF width increased, ECF height decreased, ICF width increased, ICF height decreased
options.E: ECF width increased, ECF height increased, ICF width decreased, ICF height increased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: In hyposmotic volume contraction (primary adrenal insufficiency/aldosterone deficiency), renal loss of NaCl exceeds water loss, causing a primary decrease in ECF osmolarity (height of ECF decreases) and a contraction of ECF volume. Because ECF osmolarity is now lower than ICF osmolarity, water shifts from the ECF into the ICF down its osmotic gradient until osmotic equilibrium is restored. Consequently, the ECF volume contracts further (ECF width decreases), the ICF volume expands (ICF width increases), and the final osmolarity of both compartments decreases equally (height of both ICF and ECF decreases).

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 66-year-old male with extensive-stage small cell lung carcinoma is admitted to the hospital with progressive lethargy, confusion, and generalized muscle weakness. Physical examination reveals an euvolemic state without peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, or postural hypotension. Laboratory testing demonstrates profound hyponatremia (serum sodium: 114 mEq/L; reference: 135–145 mEq/L), decreased serum osmolality (238 mOsm/kg; reference: 275–295 mOsm/kg), inappropriately elevated urine osmolality (580 mOsm/kg), and urine sodium of 48 mEq/L. A diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is established. If a Darrow-Yannet diagram representing this patient's fluid status following osmotic equilibration is compared to that of a patient experiencing primary adrenal insufficiency, which of the following physiological parameters changes in opposite directions between these two clinical conditions?

options.A: Intracellular fluid (ICF) volume
options.B: Extracellular fluid (ECF) volume
options.C: Extracellular fluid (ECF) osmolarity
options.D: Intracellular fluid (ICF) osmolarity
options.E: Red blood cell (RBC) volume

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: This multi-step question requires working through a 5-step clinical-physiological reasoning chain: (1) Diagnose the patient: small cell lung carcinoma presenting with euvolemic hyponatremia, hypo-osmolality, and concentrated urine represents SIADH; (2) Classify the fluid disturbance in SIADH: excessive ADH induces pure free water retention, producing hyposmotic volume expansion, where ECF volume increases (↑), ECF/ICF osmolarity decreases (↓), water shifts into cells expanding ICF volume (↑), and RBCs swell (↑); (3) Recall the pathophysiology of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease): lack of aldosterone causes renal salt wasting exceeding water loss, producing hyposmotic volume contraction; (4) Determine the fluid compartment shifts in adrenal insufficiency: ECF osmolarity decreases (↓), driving water into cells so ICF volume increases (↑), RBCs swell (↑), and ICF osmolarity decreases (↓), while ECF volume contracts (decreases, ↓); (5) Compare the two states: both conditions feature decreased ECF osmolarity, decreased ICF osmolarity, increased ICF volume, and increased RBC volume. However, ECF volume changes in opposite directions: it is increased (expanded) in SIADH and decreased (contracted) in primary adrenal insufficiency.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A clinical pharmacology research protocol requires accurate quantification of a subject's extracellular fluid (ECF) volume prior to dosing an experimental hydrophilic drug. An intravenous tracer is administered that distributes rapidly throughout the extracellular compartment, freely crossing capillary endothelium while remaining completely excluded from cells and resisting metabolic degradation. Which of the following substances is the standard physiological indicator used to measure ECF volume directly via indicator dilution?

options.A: Tritiated water (3H2O)
options.B: Heavy water (D2O)
options.C: Inulin
options.D: Radioiodinated serum albumin (RISA)
options.E: Evans blue dye

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Inulin (or mannitol) is a large polymer that freely crosses capillary walls to distribute evenly throughout the vascular and interstitial spaces, but cannot cross cell membranes into the intracellular compartment. Therefore, inulin distributes exclusively throughout the extracellular fluid (ECF) and serves as the classic physiological marker for direct measurement of ECF volume by indicator dilution.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department after sustaining a deep laceration to his forearm with acute moderate blood loss. He receives an intravenous infusion of 2.0 L of isotonic (0.9%) saline over 45 minutes to restore intravascular volume. Following complete equilibration, which of the following changes in extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, intracellular fluid (ICF) volume, hematocrit, and plasma protein concentration will be observed?

options.A: ECF volume increased, ICF volume unchanged, hematocrit decreased, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.B: ECF volume increased, ICF volume increased, hematocrit decreased, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.C: ECF volume increased, ICF volume decreased, hematocrit increased, plasma protein concentration unchanged
options.D: ECF volume unchanged, ICF volume increased, hematocrit decreased, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.E: ECF volume increased, ICF volume unchanged, hematocrit unchanged, plasma protein concentration increased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Infusion of isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl, ~290–300 mOsm/L) represents an isosmotic volume expansion. The added fluid is isosmotic to normal plasma, so ECF osmolarity remains unchanged. Because there is no transcellular osmotic gradient, no water shifts between ECF and ICF; thus, ICF volume and ICF osmolarity remain completely unchanged. The expansion of ECF/plasma volume dilutes intravascular solutes, causing both hematocrit and plasma protein concentration to decrease.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 50-year-old male with treatment-resistant hypertension is evaluated in the clinic. A high-sodium diet challenge is performed during which he ingests large quantities of hypertonic sodium chloride tablets over 24 hours without significant free water intake. At a new steady state, the excess sodium remains restricted to the extracellular space by active Na+/K+-ATPase pumps. Which of the following changes in fluid compartment volumes and osmolarities will occur following complete osmotic equilibration?

options.A: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume increased, osmolarity of both compartments decreased
options.B: ECF volume increased, ICF volume decreased, osmolarity of both compartments increased
options.C: ECF volume increased, ICF volume increased, osmolarity of both compartments increased
options.D: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume decreased, osmolarity of both compartments increased
options.E: ECF volume increased, ICF volume unchanged, osmolarity of both compartments unchanged

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Ingestion of hypertonic NaCl represents hyperosmotic volume expansion. The added NaCl distributes primarily in the ECF, directly elevating ECF osmolarity. This creates an osmotic gradient that draws water out of the ICF into the ECF until osmolarity equilibrates. As a result, ECF volume expands, ICF volume contracts (cells shrink), and the osmolarity of both compartments increases equally.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with persistent polydipsia and polyuria. She is discovered to have central diabetes insipidus resulting from head trauma. Daily urine output is 6.5 L with a urine osmolality of 90 mOsm/kg. Due to severe loss of dilute, hypotonic urine without adequate water replacement, her fluid balance undergoes hyperosmotic volume contraction. Which of the following lab findings is most consistent with this patient's fluid status?

options.A: Decreased serum sodium concentration, decreased hematocrit, and decreased plasma protein concentration
options.B: Elevated serum sodium concentration, elevated plasma protein concentration, and approximately unchanged hematocrit
options.C: Normal serum sodium concentration, elevated hematocrit, and elevated plasma protein concentration
options.D: Decreased serum sodium concentration, elevated hematocrit, and elevated plasma protein concentration
options.E: Elevated serum sodium concentration, decreased plasma protein concentration, and decreased hematocrit

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: In hyperosmotic volume contraction (such as diabetes insipidus or water deprivation), the primary loss of free water elevates serum sodium concentration and plasma osmolarity. Plasma protein concentration increases due to hemoconcentration within the contracted vascular space. However, hematocrit remains approximately unchanged because the hypertonic ECF draws water out of erythrocytes, causing red blood cells to shrink; the reduction in individual RBC volume counterbalances the hemoconcentrating effect of decreased plasma volume.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 29-year-old male presents to the emergency department after running a marathon on a hot, humid day. He consumed excessive amounts of plain water during and immediately after the race while sweating profusely. Physical examination reveals an alert, well-hydrated male with mild nausea and a normal blood pressure. Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum sodium concentration of 124 mEq/L (reference: 135–145 mEq/L), decreased serum osmolality (256 mOsm/kg), and a decreased hematocrit. If a Darrow-Yannet diagram is constructed to model this patient's body fluid compartments, how do the width (volume) and height (osmolarity) of his intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment compare to his pre-race baseline?

options.A: ICF width is increased and ICF height is decreased
options.B: ICF width is decreased and ICF height is increased
options.C: ICF width is unchanged and ICF height is decreased
options.D: ICF width is increased and ICF height is increased
options.E: ICF width is decreased and ICF height is decreased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: This 3rd-order question requires a 3-step reasoning chain: (1) Recognize the clinical scenario of hypotonic fluid overload (exercise-associated hyponatremia due to heavy sweating followed by massive ingestion of pure free water) as hyposmotic volume expansion; (2) Understand the osmotic shift: the excessive water intake primarily dilutes the ECF, lowering its osmolarity (decreasing ECF height). Because ECF osmolarity is now lower than ICF osmolarity, water moves down its osmotic gradient from the ECF into the ICF until a new, lower osmotic equilibrium is established; (3) Deduce the Darrow-Yannet shifts for the ICF compartment: water entering the cells expands the intracellular volume (increasing ICF width), while intracellular osmolarity decreases to match the diluted ECF (decreasing ICF height).

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 60-kg female patient is admitted to the hospital for elective orthopedic surgery. The resident calculates her baseline body fluid distribution assuming normal physiological proportions where total body water (TBW) accounts for approximately 50% of her total body weight. According to standard physiological distribution, what is the estimated volume of fluid normally contained within her extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment?
usmle_practice_problems.rationale: For an adult female with a total body water (TBW) of 50% of body weight, TBW is 30 L (0.50 x 60 kg = 30 L). Standard fluid partition dictates that extracellular fluid (ECF) represents one-third (1/3) of total body water (or 20% of body weight in typical reference models). Thus, ECF volume is 30 L x 1/3 = 10.0 L. The remaining two-thirds (2/3) resides in the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment (20.0 L).

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 30-year-old male firefighter is admitted to the burn unit after suffering third-degree thermal burns covering 35% of his total body surface area. Over the initial 12 hours, extensive transvascular capillary leakage results in the massive loss of an isosmotic, protein-rich plasma exudate into the denuded interstitial spaces and the external environment. Laboratory testing demonstrates an elevated hematocrit of 54% (baseline: 42%). Following this acute isosmotic volume contraction, which of the following describes the volume and osmolarity changes in his intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment?

options.A: ICF volume decreased, ICF osmolarity increased
options.B: ICF volume increased, ICF osmolarity decreased
options.C: ICF volume unchanged, ICF osmolarity unchanged
options.D: ICF volume decreased, ICF osmolarity unchanged
options.E: ICF volume unchanged, ICF osmolarity decreased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Severe burns cause an acute isosmotic volume contraction characterized by the loss of fluid that is isosmotic to normal plasma from the extracellular space. Although ECF volume decreases substantially, the osmolarity of the remaining ECF remains completely unchanged. Because no transcellular osmotic gradient is created between the ECF and ICF, there is no driving force for water movement across cell membranes. Consequently, ICF volume and ICF osmolarity remain entirely unchanged.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic with a 3-day history of high fever, profuse diaphoresis, and refusal to drink fluids due to painful pharyngitis. Physical examination reveals dry oral mucous membranes, sunken eyes, and lethargy. The loss of hypotonic sweat combined with water deprivation produces hyperosmotic volume contraction. A medical student reviews the patient's expected laboratory values. Which of the following changes in red blood cell (RBC) volume and plasma protein concentration is expected in this patient?

options.A: RBC volume increased, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.B: RBC volume decreased, plasma protein concentration increased
options.C: RBC volume unchanged, plasma protein concentration increased
options.D: RBC volume decreased, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.E: RBC volume increased, plasma protein concentration increased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: In hyperosmotic volume contraction (such as unreplaced sweating, fever, or water deprivation), the primary deficit is the loss of hypotonic fluid (excess free water loss relative to solute). This elevates the osmolarity of the extracellular fluid (ECF). The hypertonic ECF draws water out of intracellular compartments down its osmotic gradient, causing cells, including erythrocytes, to shrink (RBC volume decreases). Concurrently, the reduction in extracellular fluid volume hemoconcentrates circulating macromolecules, causing plasma protein concentration to increase.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 19-year-old female presents to the university health clinic with fatigue and orthostatic dizziness. She has been consuming a strict zero-salt fad diet for four weeks while taking an over-the-counter herbal diuretic that promotes renal natriuresis without water restriction. This combination causes persistent renal sodium wasting that markedly exceeds water loss, establishing a state of hyposmotic volume contraction. Which of the following sets of changes in hematocrit and plasma protein concentration will be observed in this patient?

options.A: Hematocrit increased, plasma protein concentration increased
options.B: Hematocrit decreased, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.C: Hematocrit unchanged, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.D: Hematocrit increased, plasma protein concentration decreased
options.E: Hematocrit decreased, plasma protein concentration increased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: In hyposmotic volume contraction (such as excessive renal salt wasting or adrenal insufficiency), loss of NaCl exceeds water loss, causing ECF osmolarity to decrease. Water shifts down the osmotic gradient from the hyposmotic ECF into the ICF. This causes a dual contraction of the vascular/ECF space: first from external fluid loss and second from transcellular shift into cells. The marked decrease in plasma volume hemoconcentrates plasma proteins, so plasma protein concentration increases. Concurrently, hematocrit increases profoundly due to two reinforcing factors: the decrease in plasma volume concentrates erythrocytes, and the hypoosmotic environment causes water to enter erythrocytes, swelling them (increasing individual RBC volume). Both factors drive hematocrit upward.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 58-year-old male with a history of alcohol use disorder presents to the hospital after consuming a massive quantity of highly concentrated salty broth and pretzels without drinking water, precipitating hyperosmotic volume expansion. At the same time, another patient in the clinical unit with small cell lung carcinoma develops severe hyponatremia due to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), representing hyposmotic volume expansion. Both patients have reached complete transcellular osmotic equilibration. If Darrow-Yannet diagrams representing their respective fluid states are compared against each other, which of the following physiological parameters shifts in the SAME direction in both patients relative to normal baseline?

options.A: Intracellular fluid (ICF) volume
options.B: Extracellular fluid (ECF) volume
options.C: Extracellular fluid (ECF) osmolarity
options.D: Intracellular fluid (ICF) osmolarity
options.E: Red blood cell (RBC) volume

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: This multi-step question requires working through a 5-step physiological reasoning sequence: (1) Identify Patient 1's condition: massive ingestion of hypertonic salt without water causes hyperosmotic volume expansion; (2) Determine fluid shifts for hyperosmotic volume expansion: added NaCl increases ECF osmolarity (↑), drawing water from the ICF into the ECF, which expands ECF volume (↑), contracts ICF volume (↓), shrinks erythrocytes (↓ RBC volume), and increases osmolarity in both compartments (↑); (3) Identify Patient 2's condition: SIADH induces pure water retention, causing hyposmotic volume expansion; (4) Determine fluid shifts for hyposmotic volume expansion: retained free water expands ECF volume (↑) and dilutes ECF osmolarity (↓), driving water from the ECF into the ICF, which expands ICF volume (↑), swells erythrocytes (↑ RBC volume), and decreases osmolarity in both compartments (↓); (5) Compare the directional shifts between the two states: ICF volume (decreased in hyperosmotic vs. increased in hyposmotic), ECF osmolarity (increased vs. decreased), ICF osmolarity (increased vs. decreased), and RBC volume (decreased vs. increased) all shift in opposite directions. Only extracellular fluid (ECF) volume shifts in the same direction, expanding (increasing, ↑) in both conditions.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A clinical physiologist is validating an indicator dilution protocol to determine a subject's vascular plasma volume before administering an experimental monoclonal antibody. An indicator is chosen that binds strongly to circulating plasma proteins, is largely retained within the capillary network, and does not penetrate into the interstitial space or cellular compartments. Which of the following substances is the standard physiological indicator used to measure plasma volume directly?

options.A: Tritiated water (3H2O)
options.B: Inulin
options.C: Radioiodinated serum albumin (RISA)
options.D: Mannitol
options.E: Heavy water (D2O)

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Radioiodinated serum albumin (RISA) or Evans blue dye binds tightly to serum albumin and is confined almost entirely to the intravascular vascular compartment (plasma) because albumin does not readily cross healthy continuous capillary endothelium. Therefore, RISA directly measures plasma volume by indicator dilution.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 24-year-old female presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident resulting in severe pelvic fractures and acute intra-abdominal hemorrhage. She loses approximately 1.2 L of whole blood prior to arrival. Physical examination reveals hypotension (BP 82/50 mmHg), tachycardia (HR 125 bpm), and cool, pale extremities. Which of the following combinations of changes in extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, intracellular fluid (ICF) volume, and serum osmolarity is present immediately following this acute hemorrhage prior to significant transcapillary refill or fluid resuscitation?

options.A: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume unchanged, serum osmolarity unchanged
options.B: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume decreased, serum osmolarity increased
options.C: ECF volume decreased, ICF volume increased, serum osmolarity decreased
options.D: ECF volume unchanged, ICF volume decreased, serum osmolarity unchanged
options.E: ECF volume increased, ICF volume unchanged, serum osmolarity unchanged

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Acute blood loss (hemorrhage) represents an isosmotic volume contraction. Whole blood is removed directly from the intravascular component of the extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment. Because whole blood and its plasma are isosmotic to normal body fluids, the osmolarity of the remaining ECF is unchanged. With no osmotic gradient established across cell membranes, no fluid shifts into or out of cells; thus, ICF volume and serum osmolarity remain unchanged.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 49-year-old male is admitted to the intensive care unit with severe cerebral edema following a traumatic head injury. To rapidly reduce intracranial pressure, the neurointensivist orders an intravenous infusion of 20% hypertonic mannitol. Mannitol is an osmotically active carbohydrate that freely traverses the vascular endothelium into the extracellular fluid but cannot penetrate intact cell membranes. What immediate transcellular fluid shift and changes in fluid compartment volumes will occur following administration of this hypertonic solution?

options.A: Water shifts from ECF to ICF; ECF volume decreases and ICF volume increases
options.B: Water shifts from ICF to ECF; ECF volume increases and ICF volume decreases
options.C: No fluid shifts occur; both ECF and ICF volumes expand equally
options.D: Solutes shift from ICF to ECF; both ECF and ICF volumes remain unchanged
options.E: Water shifts from ICF to ECF; both ECF and ICF volumes increase

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Infusion of hypertonic mannitol represents hyperosmotic volume expansion. Because mannitol remains confined to the extracellular fluid (ECF), it directly elevates ECF osmolarity. The resulting osmotic gradient draws water rapidly out of cells (ICF) into the ECF until osmotic equilibrium is re-established. Consequently, intracellular fluid (ICF) volume decreases (causing brain cells to shrink and reducing intracranial pressure) while extracellular fluid (ECF) volume expands.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 54-year-old female with a history of recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis is prescribed a high dose of hydrochlorothiazide. Over several weeks, she consumes large amounts of plain water while experiencing continuous drug-induced renal sodium chloride wasting that markedly exceeds water excretion. She presents with fatigue, confusion, and muscle cramps. Laboratory studies reveal a low serum sodium level of 122 mEq/L (hyponatremia) and reduced plasma osmolality. What effect will this hyposmotic state have on erythrocyte volume and hematocrit?

options.A: Erythrocytes shrink, causing hematocrit to decrease
options.B: Erythrocytes swell, and hematocrit increases significantly
options.C: Erythrocyte volume remains unchanged, and hematocrit is normal
options.D: Erythrocytes swell, but hematocrit decreases due to plasma expansion
options.E: Erythrocytes shrink, but hematocrit increases due to splenic contraction

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: In hyposmotic volume contraction (such as excessive thiazide or diuretic-induced salt wasting), loss of sodium chloride exceeds water loss, decreasing ECF osmolarity. Water moves down the osmotic gradient from the hyposmotic ECF into the ICF, including red blood cells, causing erythrocytes to swell (increasing individual RBC volume). At the same time, the dual loss of ECF volume (from urinary loss and internal fluid shift into cells) causes severe hemoconcentration of the vascular space. Because decreased plasma volume and increased RBC volume act synergistically, hematocrit increases significantly.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Physiology: Body Fluid Compartments, Volume Expansions and Contractions
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 35-year-old male with untreated primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) experiences chronic autonomous aldosterone secretion. Aldosterone promotes continuous renal distal tubular sodium reabsorption. The patient drinks water ad libitum, retaining isosmotic fluid within his extracellular compartment while maintaining a normal serum sodium concentration of 142 mEq/L and normal serum osmolality of 290 mOsm/kg. If a Darrow-Yannet diagram is constructed to assess this patient's fluid status following volume expansion, which of the following diagrams correctly reflects the changes in the width (volume) and height (osmolarity) of his ECF and ICF compartments relative to normal baseline?

options.A: ECF width is increased, ECF height is unchanged; ICF width and ICF height are unchanged
options.B: ECF width is increased, ECF height is increased; ICF width is decreased, ICF height is increased
options.C: ECF width is increased, ECF height is decreased; ICF width is increased, ICF height is decreased
options.D: ECF width is decreased, ECF height is unchanged; ICF width and ICF height are unchanged
options.E: ECF width is unchanged, ECF height is increased; ICF width is decreased, ICF height is increased

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: This 3rd-order question requires a 3-step reasoning chain: (1) Identify the underlying fluid disturbance: autonomous aldosterone production causes net renal retention of sodium and water in roughly isotonic proportions, creating an isosmotic volume expansion (similar to chronic isotonic saline infusion); (2) Determine the transcellular osmotic driving force: because the retained fluid is isosmotic to normal plasma, ECF osmolarity remains normal (height of ECF is unchanged), meaning no transcellular osmotic gradient is generated; (3) Deduce the Darrow-Yannet shifts: with no osmotic gradient, water does not move between the compartments, so ICF volume (ICF width) and ICF osmolarity (ICF height) remain entirely unchanged, while ECF volume expands (ECF width increases).
